worst_places.quote: `functools.partial(print, file=sys.stderr)` evaluates `sys.stderr` **once**, at the moment the `partial` object itself is created (at module import time), and permanently stores that specific object as the `file` keyword argument for every future call. pytest's `capsys` fixture works by temporarily **replacing** the `sys.stderr` attribute (rebinding the name `sys.stderr` to a new interceptor object) for the duration of the test — but the already-created `partial` object still holds a reference to the OLD `sys.stderr` object from import time, and keeps writing to it regardless of what `sys.stderr` gets rebound to afterward.

worst_places.after: `@dataclass` is different from a plain function: it **knows what its fields mean**. While generating `__init__`, the decorator reads the declared default values. The reason: in a dataclass, a field with a mutable default shared by every instance is almost always a mistake, not a choice.

patterns: The RU version is a translation of the EN version, and the translation leaks in six places across five chapters — «nothing works» and «historically argparse позволял» (ch 00), «compiler вынужден определять» (ch 03), «где curates публичный API» (ch 05), «С relatively недавним предложением» (ch 06), «machinально» and «баг molчит» (ch 08). Each sits at exactly the position its English counterpart occupies in the EN file, and two of them are broken mid-word (Latin stem + Cyrillic suffix). Three markup typos cluster with them: a misplaced closing quote in ru/06 (`примитив "поверх" \`try/finally",`), a stray pipe in ru/08 (`` `path.open()|) ``), and a lost agreement in ru/05 («дефолтная автообнаружение … рассчитано»). This is not a style problem — it is a QA gap, and it is the fastest fix with the highest payoff in the zone.

Language complexity drifts monotonically upward as the chapters get harder, in both locales — the same drift the `python` question bank showed at the junior→middle boundary, but smooth rather than a sharp seam. Long sentences: RU 17%→34% (ch 01→09), EN 24%→46% (ch 01→07). Over-long paragraphs: RU 2→9, EN 2→9. The break point is chapter 03-04, where EN crosses 39% and never comes back; RU crosses 26% at ch 04 and never comes back. Chapters 00-02 read cleanly for the target reader; chapters 05, 08 and 09 do not. The content did not get harder proportionally — the sentences did, because each new fact was appended to the existing sentence with an em-dash instead of starting a new one.

Zero diagrams and one table across all 20 files. The site has a diagram convention and this course uses none of it, which is why the flag script counts 52 theory walls. The most defensible cost is chapter 05, the most abstract chapter in the zone: it argues at length that «относительные импорты считают уровни пакетной иерархии, а не буквальные шаги по файловой системе» — a claim about two trees that differ — and never draws either tree. The second cost is structural: every chapter's «Частая ошибка» section is two 10-to-16-line prose paragraphs with no code at all, sitting at the end of a chapter that has otherwise taught the reader entirely through runnable examples.

The JS bridge is the course's strongest and most consistent asset and must not be touched. Every chapter opens each theory block by naming the JS reflex that will mislead the reader, and every chapter closes theory with an explicit «Параллели с JS/TS/Node» list. Rubric C is a flat 4.0 across all 20 files because of this: bolded term, then the point, then the caveats. The «Ключевые решения» bullets after each worked solution do the same job for code. Nothing in the refactor should change section structure — only sentence length inside it.
notes: Course-format adjustments applied as instructed; they moved A and E up, not down. On A: LEGB (ch 03), ABC (ch 04) and AST (ch 09) are expanded inline and are false positives from the script — the real misses are CLI (used 10x in the ch 00 title and never spelled out anywhere in the course), REPL, TC39 and PEP. On E: chapters 06, 07 and 09 explicitly state which files are unchanged since the previous chapter, which is exactly what the course rubric asks for — but they then print only the changed files, so the full project state exists nowhere after chapter 05, and a reader returning after a week to ch 07 must reconstruct `cli/parser.py` and `cli/app.py` from two chapters back. Three theory snippets are also not self-contained: ch 06's `FileLock` uses `fcntl` with no `import fcntl`, ch 07's `partial` example uses `sys.stderr` with no `import sys`, ch 08's `db_connection` references an undefined `DB_PATH`. One term genuinely appears before the chapter that owns it: SQL, first used in ch 07 (`itertools.groupby` vs "SQL GROUP BY"), introduced in ch 08.
